title: C# async and await Task ValueTask cancellation and continuation context
concepts: Asynchronous programming represents work that may finish later without forcing the caller's thread to wait. `async` and `await` let code express the Task-based Asynchronous Pattern (TAP); they do not automatically create a new thread or make CPU work parallel.

A `Task` represents an operation's eventual completion, failure, or cancellation; `Task<T>` also carries a result. An async method runs synchronously until it reaches an incomplete awaitable, then its continuation resumes when the awaited operation completes.

Awaiting propagates results and exceptions through the call chain. Await tasks rather than synchronously blocking with `Wait` or `Result`; start independent I/O operations before awaiting them together, and bound concurrency when workload size is unbounded.

Cancellation is a cooperative request carried by `CancellationToken`. The operation that owns a `CancellationTokenSource` requests cancellation; callees observe and honor the token at meaningful boundaries. Cancellation does not forcibly terminate arbitrary code.

A continuation may resume through a captured `SynchronizationContext` or `TaskScheduler`. UI code usually needs its UI context; reusable library code may opt out with `ConfigureAwait(false)`. Context capture affects continuation placement, not whether the operation itself is asynchronous.

Use `ValueTask<T>` only when its allocation or synchronous-completion benefits are measured and its single-consumption rules can be respected. Prefer `Task<T>` for ordinary APIs and cacheable, repeatably awaitable operations.

`Task.WaitAsync` was introduced in .NET 6; TimeProvider overloads arrived in .NET 8. .NET 8 added CancellationTokenSource.CancelAsync, and .NET 9 added ReadOnlySpan<CancellationToken> linked-source creation. These APIs affect waiting and cancellation coordination, not the core async/await language model.

accuracyFacts: Task.Yield returns YieldAwaitable. Awaiting it posts continuation to the current SynchronizationContext or, absent one, the current TaskScheduler; it does not guarantee UI responsiveness or a particular thread.
TaskCreationOptions.RunContinuationsAsynchronously causes continuations registered to the task to run asynchronously; it does not promise they run on the thread pool.
TaskContinuationOptions.ExecuteSynchronously requests inline continuation execution; the scheduler may schedule it instead, and RunContinuationsAsynchronously takes precedence.
Task and ValueTask describe operation outcomes and may be pending, completed, faulted, or canceled; the type alone does not mean execution is currently underway.

A Task can be awaited repeatedly. ValueTask consumption constraints depend on its backing source; some IValueTaskSource-backed instances are single-consumption, but not every ValueTask is inherently single-use.
Task.WaitAsync cancellation cancels the wait operation, not necessarily the underlying task.
TaskCompletionSource RunContinuationsAsynchronously is often a useful defensive choice for producer APIs, but it is not an absolute requirement for every use.
The default Task awaiter captures a non-default SynchronizationContext, or a non-default TaskScheduler when no such SynchronizationContext is present; ExecutionContext flows separately.

ConfigureAwait(false) opts out of captured SynchronizationContext or non-default TaskScheduler resumption for that await; it does not suppress ExecutionContext or guarantee a thread switch, speedup, or deadlock prevention.

Task.WhenAll does not start its input tasks. Its returned task retains all faults in its Exception aggregate; awaiting it throws an exception, and callers needing every failure should inspect the aggregate.
async void exceptions are propagated through the SynchronizationContext active when the method starts; callers cannot catch them through a returned Task, and host behavior determines the outcome.

CancellationToken.ThrowIfCancellationRequested throws OperationCanceledException carrying that token. TaskCanceledException is a derived subtype and is not guaranteed as the exception subtype from every canceled operation.
CancellationTokenSource.CancelAsync sets cancellation-requested state and returns a Task that completes when registered callbacks finish; it is not a request that automatically stops the operation.

Task and ValueTask are reference and value types respectively, but neither type guarantees a fresh allocation per operation; ValueTask can avoid a Task allocation for some synchronous completions and has source-dependent consumption constraints.
